transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-24
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Carlos (Acme CTO), Priya (Lead ML Eng), Liam (SRE)
Artifacts shared: demo deck (link: drive.redwood/demo-edgecases.pdf), benchmark spreadsheet (link: drive.acme/benchmarks), security packet (link: redwood/security-packet.pdf)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. This is Maya from Redwood, AE. With me is Jordan, our SE. We want to run through an edge-cases demo focusing on long context, high TPS, streaming backpressure and timeouts, and then talk POC next steps. Carlos, Priya, Liam, thanks for making time.
[00:18] Carlos: Yeah thanks, Maya. Quick context: our product annotates long clinical notes and we sometimes stream 20k tokens per request, and then we also have spikes — like 1.5k requests per second for short summaries. So curious about handling long context + high TPS concurrently.
[00:35] Jordan: Perfect. We'll show both ends: long context memory and how our runtime deals with KV cache and chunked context, and then a high TPS run with batching/backpressure controls. We'll also demo streaming with simulated slow clients to show backpressure and timeouts.
[00:50] Priya: Good — also we need to know encryption at rest (KMS) and network isolation. We can't send PHI to hosted unless it's encrypted and we have a contract.
[01:05] Maya: Understood. We'll cover Redwood Private options and Dedicated pools for isolation. We'll also point you to our SOC 2 docs and KMS integrations.
[01:15] Jordan: Ok first slide quick architecture: runtime selects kernels, manages KV cache, does continuous batching. Note: sometimes the transcript tool flips KV cache to "K V cache" or "KV cash" so sorry if that shows up.
[01:30] Jordan: Demo step one: long context. I'm going to push a 18k-token clinical note into Redwood API using the same model family you use (we'll anonymize). Watch memory and latency.
[01:44] [screen share noises]
[01:50] Jordan: Sending request now... initial tokenization and chunking happens client-side for very long prompts unless you opt in to server chunking; Redwood can do both. We're showing server side chunking with prefix caching enabled.
[02:05] Priya: Wait, server chunking — does that reassemble on-the-fly or stream partial outputs? For us we need deterministic ordering and we want ability to resume interrupted requests.
[02:18] Jordan: Great question. We stream partial outputs as they're generated; for deterministic reassembly we include chunk meta headers with sequence ids. Resume is supported via a resume token that references KV cache state — note: in Hosted we manage resume tokens, in Dedicated/Private you can persist them locally for audit.
[02:40] Liam: How large can the KV cache grow? If we have 18k tokens per user and say 10k concurrent sessions, that's huge.
[02:50] Jordan: For memory control we recommend prefix eviction strategies and per-session caps. In Dedicated, you can tune max KV per session and enable LRU eviction. Also we have transparent offload to CPU/GPU host memory and quantized cache entries to save space. Performance tradeoffs apply.
[03:10] Carlos: That tradeoff — how much latency hit when evicting or offloading?
[03:16] Jordan: Our benchmarks show typical 5-20ms extra per-request when offloading cold cache pages, but it varies by model/attention length. In the spreadsheet I just dropped, you can see numbers on the right (note: the live sheet had a small typo — 5ms row labeled 50ms).
[03:32] Maya: Moving to high TPS. We'll simulate 1.2k RPS of short prompt completions. Jordan, kick the load test.
[03:40] Jordan: Running load test now. We're targeting a Dedicated pool with autoscale and burst capacity. Important: continuous batching will group small requests to improve GPU utilization while keeping p95 latency low.
[03:52] [synthetic load noise / terminal output]
[03:55] Priya: We're interested in tail latency — what's p99 under sustained 1.2k RPS?
[04:02] Jordan: Under the config shown (batch size cap 32, latency SLO 150ms), p99 was ~220ms in our internal run, but with smaller models and aggressive batching it can approach 150ms. We also had a p99 spike when GC kicked in — we recommend pinning processes and using realtime kernels in Dedicated to avoid that.
[04:24] Liam: What about backpressure to upstream clients when GPU saturated? We have many mobile clients with variable network.
[04:32] Jordan: We surfaced backpressure at the API layer. Options: 1) Return 429 with Retry-After, 2) queue with a short TTL, 3) stream partial tokens with a "stall" event so client knows server is busy. For streaming backpressure we prefer the stall+resume pattern rather than dropping connections.
[04:52] Carlos: Does the streaming stall pattern require client changes? We have a mobile SDK.
[04:58] Jordan: Minimal change: handle a stall frame and keep the socket open. In our SDKs we expose retry/resume helpers. Older clients can fall back to 429 behavior.
[05:10] Priya: How do timeouts interplay? If client-side timeout occurs but server finished later, do you persist the result?
[05:18] Jordan: By default, server doesn't persist on client timeout for ephemeral tokens. But in Dedicated/Private you can enable server-side persistence or enable a callback webhook to receive completion asynchronously. We recommend the async webhook for unreliable client links.
[05:36] Maya: I'm going to trigger a simulated slow client now to show streaming backpressure. Jordan, make the server slow to emit tokens to simulate network slowness.
[05:44] [demo audible 'typing' and terminal noise]
[05:50] Jordan: Slowing emitter... you can see the stall frames in the stream: "[STALL] backpressure: queued=84". The client stayed connected; the frontend shows a spinner then resumed once backlog cleared.
[06:08] Liam: What happens if our mobile client gives up after 10s? Do we cancel server compute or continue?
[06:14] Jordan: Cleanup behavior is configurable: default is to continue compute for short TTL (to serve webhooks), but you can set early-cancel-on-disconnect to free GPU. For cost-sensitive workloads we recommend early cancel on disconnect plus async persistence for critical tasks.
[06:30] Carlos: Can we implement per-route SLOs? Eg summaries route prioritized over full note processing during spikes?
[06:36] Jordan: Yes — smart routing lets you set route priority, region routing, and fallback to cheaper model variant automatically. We can also set QoS so that summaries get dispatched to a hot pool while long contexts go to a reserve pool.
[06:50] Priya: About model variants — if we fall back to a quantized variant, how do we detect regression in output quality?
[06:58] Jordan: Redwood Optimize ties quality monitoring to your eval sets. We run continuous evals on prompt sets and surface regressions; can trigger rollback or notify. You can also pin routes to particular model versions if you want strict control.
[07:14] Maya: Let's pivot to security: Priya, you mentioned KMS and PHI. We support customer-managed KMS in Private and Dedicated; for Hosted we offer envelope encryption with HSM-backed keys and controlled export. We also provide audit logs and SSO/SAML integration.
[07:32] Priya: How granular are audit logs — do they include prompt text by default?
[07:38] Jordan: We have configurable logging. For PHI you can disable prompt persistence and only keep hashed metadata; for PII-heavy workflows we recommend Private deployment so logs never leave your VPC.
[07:52] Liam: Network topology: do you support VPC peering or PrivateLink?
[07:58] Maya: Yes — PrivateLink and VPC peering are supported for Dedicated and Private. We'll share the network diagram in the security packet link.
[08:08] Carlos: Pricing — what does a Dedicated pool that handles 1.2k RPS for small models and can also serve bursts of long-context jobs cost?
[08:18] Maya: Pricing is usage plus reserved node commitments. We estimate a mid-size cluster plus burst buffer; I'll include an example cost run in the bench sheet. Exact quote requires workload specifics; we'll follow up.
[08:30] Jordan: Quick note on kernel switching — when sequence lengths vary a lot, runtime chooses different kernels; that can cause jitter. We mitigate via sequence bucketing and prewarm lanes.
[08:44] Priya: Any known issues with streaming + quantization? We had artifacts before where streaming truncated tokens when using 4-bit kernels.
[08:52] Jordan: There were older drivers where certain attention kernels had tokenization boundary bugs with 4-bit mixed kernels; we've patched recent releases. For safety we can pin a variant that avoids that kernel. We'll include patch notes in the security packet.
[09:08] [longish demo run; load test output continues]
[09:20] Maya: Ok recap: we demonstrated long context handling (chunking + KV cache + resume tokens), high TPS with continuous batching and p99 numbers, streaming backpressure patterns (stall+resume, 429 alternatives), timeout and persistence patterns, and security options (KMS, VPC, Private).
[09:36] Carlos: This was great. For POC we want: 1) Dedicated pool sized for our peak, 2) a week of integrated load testing with our mobile SDK, 3) security review and SOC2 attestation review.
[09:48] Maya: Sounds good. Proposed POC kickoff: 2026-07-06 with SE + SRE. We'll provide bench spreadsheet, network diagram, and a small sample of code to exercise resume tokens and streaming stall handling.
[09:58] Priya: Also want example config for early-cancel-on-disconnect and on-server persistence webhooks.
[10:04] Jordan: I'll push example config and a sample webhooks handler in the repo link.
[10:10] Liam: One last question — if our mobile client upgrades mid-run, how does the resume token compatibility work?
[10:18] Jordan: Resume tokens are versioned; server will attempt to map old tokens to current session state when possible; we maintain a token compatibility table and can do graceful migration in Dedicated.
[10:30] Maya: All right, thanks everyone. We'll send follow ups: bench sheet, SOC2 + network doc, POC checklist, and a calendar invite for 7/6.
[10:40] Carlos: Thanks, Maya/Jordan. Appreciate the thorough demo.
[10:44] Maya: Thanks all — talk soon.
